title: Year four close: the schools
hookLine: many schools, taught in their own words, none ranked

cards: On one street in some big cities, you can pass a Thai temple with a gold-tipped roof, a Zen center in a converted house with shoes lined up by the door, a Chinese temple where the name of Amitabha is chanted, and a Tibetan center with prayer flags strung over the porch.
Different doors, different shoes at each one. To a newcomer, they can look like four separate religions. Today, the last day of year four, they open onto rooms you've spent a year walking through.

teach.h: MANY DOORS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.
teach.b: First, the doors. Each school came in by its own door, in its own words. The Theravada's Abhidhamma, taking the mind apart moment by moment.
The Mahayana sutras, with their burning houses and rooms full of seats. Zen: sit down and see. Pure Land: call the name and trust.

The Tibetan schools, with renunciation, compassion and the diamond path all at once. Tiantai and Huayan, Nichiren and Won, Ambedkar's new vehicle, and teachers carrying it all into hospitals and forests.
Second: none of them was ranked. Not because the schools agree on everything. They don't.

They differ on which texts are the Buddha's word, on sudden or gradual awakening, on the arahant and the bodhisattva, on what the Pure Land is. Each answers for itself, with its own teachers and reasons.
This path's job was to let each one speak, and to say who says what. As day thirteen seventy-eight put it, each one has carried people across. Third, the house.
Behind all those doors, this year kept finding the same rooms. The four truths. The three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha.
Precepts, meditation, kindness. A bow, a breath, a lamp. A verse about avoiding harm, doing good and clearing the mind, carried on a full moon in Thailand and up a pine tree in China.
Many doors: the schools, each whole in itself. One house: the ground they stand on together, which each school would describe in its own words.
Fourth: year five opens with a little Pali, the language of the Theravada canon and its chants, then the sources themselves, read slowly, with a path to live.

how: A Buddhist may practice within one school and its teachers and still visit other temples, join gatherings across schools, or keep shared festivals alongside Buddhists of other schools.

games.q: you're on a street with a Thai temple, a Zen center, a Chinese temple and a Tibetan center. what does this path ask you to do with them?
o: let each speak in its own words, and say who says what.
games.why: this year let each school speak for itself, named the differences, and ranked none.

practice: Turn toward the nearest door or window and let your eyes rest on it without naming anything. Think of all the doors this year opened, without choosing between them, and let them stand open.
Then let your attention go out through the nearest one, over the street, the roofs, the sky, and when it's ready, back to the breath, here, inside the house.

wordCard.voice: Year four close. The end of the year of the schools: the Abhidhamma, the Mahayana sutras, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions and the movements, each in its own words, none ranked. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many doors, one house. Each school whole in itself, and none ranked. Year four, complete.
